questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=5$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(0))+C \\ 1 & =-1+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=5.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =2(0)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(0))+K \\ K & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+5.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=2{e}^{2t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x={e}^{2}$ and velocity $v={e}^{2}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 2{e}^{2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{2t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)={e}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & ={e}^{2(1)}+C \\ {e}^{2} & ={e}^{2}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)={e}^{2t}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{2t}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1)={e}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1)}+K \\ {e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Using a Joint PDF
questions.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3},\, & 0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(Y<X<Y+2).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=[0,3]\times [0,1],$ and the event $A={Y<X<Y+2}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/f4a0cc357eee835c84ef08524d27e3c30b98d58e1b6b5083b7df6a66ce987b6b.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<X<Y+2) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{A}\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{Area}(A) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Components of Acceleration at a Particular Moment
questions.problem: The velocity $v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=⟨-{t}^{2},\,1,\,t⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=1\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{N}=\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||}.
$$

First, we evaluate $v(1):$

$$
v(1)=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩
$$

Next, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector and evaluating it at $t=1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,0,\,1⟩, \\ a(1) & =⟨-2,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $v(1)\times a(1),||v(1)||,$ and $||v(1)\times a(1)||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1)\times a(1) & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩\times ⟨-2,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =⟨1,-1,2⟩, \\ ||v(1)|| & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}, \\ ||v(1)\times a(1)|| & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the normal component of the acceleration at $t=1,$ and we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =\frac{||v(1)\times a(1)||}{||v(1)||} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal component of acceleration is $\sqrt{2}\,{\text{ms}}^{-2}.$

questions.problem: The velocity $v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=0\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{N}=\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||}.
$$

First, we evaluate $v(0):$

$$
v(0)=⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩
$$

Next, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector and evaluating it at $t=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩, \\ a(0) & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $v(0)\times a(0),||v(0)||,$ and $||v(0)\times a(0)||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0)\times a(0) & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =⟨1,-1,0⟩, \\ ||v(0)|| & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}, \\ ||v(0)\times a(0)|| & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the normal component of the acceleration at $t=0,$ and we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =\frac{||v(0)\times a(0)||}{||v(0)||} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal component of acceleration is $1\,{\text{ms}}^{-2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima of a Function Whose Domain Is Piecewise Smooth
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/e0331b5d4c9fa3c823d6596c1ab147b8ee459feb4a4feaed3c614e2639ae77e5.png)

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=4x-xy$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 4-{x}^{2}},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4-y,\,-x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4-y=0 \\ -x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=4\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,4).$ Since the point $(0,4)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =4(t)-(t)(0) \\  & =4t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =4(t)-(t)(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3})^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives one solution, $t=0,$ inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$
Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain the candidate point, $(0,4).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,4),\,(2,0),\,(-2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $8$ | $-8$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-8$ at the point $(-2,0)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $8$ at the points $(2,0).$

questions.problem: Find the global maximum of the function $f(x,y)=x+y-xy$ on the closed triangular region $D$ with vertices $(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-y & 1-x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}1-y=0 \\ 1-x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,1).$ Since the point $(1,1)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,1).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =t+0-t(0) \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t⟨1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,t) \\  & =t+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,1),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (2t-{t}^{2})^{′} & =0 \\ 2-2t & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t=1$ does not belong to the range $t\in (0,1),$ we do not include the corresponding point in the list of candidates for extrema.

- The line connecting $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(1,t) \\  & =1+t-t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total, we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(1,1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(1,1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(0,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the points $(1,0)$ and $(1,1).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux in a Source-Free Vector Field
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/698d8b5bb0d12e85bbde7559bf1bc61de6bb9abdadfe788b22d1431eb3a71582.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(0,4)$ and $B(5,2).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2xy\,i-{y}^{2}\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{2})=2y-2y=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(0,4)$ to $B(5,2)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/40bf4e64da0d4d9cb66e6e83d7275d4a44180a93341c413a5df720263469bfdc.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =4\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+2j)-(4\,j)] \\  & =5t\,i+(4-2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2xy=2(5t)(4-2t)=40t-20{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =-{y}^{2}=-(4-2t)^{2}=-16+16t-4{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)=5, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-2t)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((40t-20{t}^{2})\cdot (-2)-(-16+16t-4{t}^{2})\cdot (5))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,60{t}^{2}-160t+80\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[20{t}^{3}-80{t}^{2}+80t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=20.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/ab4dc3ae0e3a62fc255a4bc066ae58c58f64546161466e4db474e39486492a53.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+t\cdot [(2\,i+4\,j)-(2\,i+\,j)] \\  & =2\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-3\sqrt{y}=-3\sqrt{3t+1}, \\ Q(x,y) & =3\sqrt{x}=3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3\sqrt{3t+1})\cdot (3)-(3\sqrt{2})\cdot (0)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-9(3t+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-2(3t+1)^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-14.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=⟨z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2x)-(0)\cdot (-2y)+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between Two Parallel Axes
questions.problem:
A circular plate of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ with uniform mass density occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $2\,\text{m}$ and is centered at the origin.
Given that the moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $15\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2},$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass of $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

The area of the circular plate $D$ is $A=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi \,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{3}{4\pi }\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid $(0,0).$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }\cdot 4\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =6\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 15 & =6+3{d}^{2} \\ 3{d}^{2} & =9 \\ {d}^{2} & =3 \\ d & =\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A circular plate of mass $1\,\text{kg}$ with uniform mass density occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ and is centered at the origin.
Given that the moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2},$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass of $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{6},\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

The area of the circular plate $D$ is $A=\pi \cdot (\sqrt{6})^{2}=6\pi \,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{1}{6\pi }\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid $(0,0).$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot 9\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =3\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 4 & =3+1{d}^{2} \\ {d}^{2} & =1 \\ d & =1\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/53b96d29aaddea4971bc14207fa153613f2492b123c4de70d14161b3f6a17df8.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2y,$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =2y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =2\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/cd499dfb1a27171f56e9d253e42fec5884260adef1f8ca5e9e2cecd5a4fb45da.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ[\rho ]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ-0)\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & ={[ϕ-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =(\pi -0)\cdot (1+1) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Change the order of integration in the integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ and then $z.$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/e32a019900b77c0bb84b4599b8899e3d0d32ae07d9674da126db34394b97ea24.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/af629672ff2fd31eeae585ad4941fb8682941444cd34383392fb0a6bec24396e.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/04dc917237ab002263e35fb4a84c264fef240fefaa456c5249d6e24d0c8ebe28.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/b2a6fc02441bb6013b6f54d49ceefafc1468b291ae4149847290135bbf2d2e56.png)

We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by 

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/b942dbfba8276421620df6258c9951c2b91a5d2dea18c84260c90b6cbe6f760b.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ then $z,$ we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arctan}⁡x}^{\pi /4}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.

questions.problem:
Change the order of integration in the following integral, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $z,$ then $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,{y}^{3}\le z\le 2}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type I region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{2}}.
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/58a9056015b3dad91ec7ae64bff893c8c6c2cce6480c979545e423cbe105ef03.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where ${y}^{3}\le z\le 2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/2fdd6a15b4ddadfc3ee24af5e35e2a87e9e963ceeefbf858b704d78ee0b78513.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/65da730d32f200b8f9da004ee8cf6b7e79095e323961f4a5b6dfa0bddeace42b.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=(x,z),$ is

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt[3]{z}
$$

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{z}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/1743f540a85fc1c266c84da8f34b2012516b7bbc98d113cf7c62ba3bba8173c1.png)

We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by 

$$
z=(\sqrt[3]{2})^{3}=2.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/b76bf84e1179bec6a1e8e357c6cc628eee95c1663e6f0ff375135612a6f275de.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,0\le z\le 2}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}f(x,y,z)\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Volume of a Region Using a Change of Variables
questions.problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,\frac{1}{2}\le x\le 1,\,3\le y+{x}^{2}\le 10,\,1\le xz\le 2}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
\frac{1}{2}\le x\le 1,\,3\le y+{x}^{2}\le 10,\,1\le xz\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=y+{x}^{2},\,w=xz.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,\frac{1}{2}\le u\le 1,\,3\le v\le 10,\,1\le w\le 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2x & 1 & 0 \\ z & 0 & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =x \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |\frac{1}{u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{3}^{10}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{u}du\cdot {\int }_{3}^{10}dv\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}dw \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{u=1/2}^{u=1}\cdot [v]_{v=3}^{v=10}\cdot [w]_{w=1}^{w=2} \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})\cdot (10-3)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le {x}^{2}-y-z\le 1,\,1\le \sqrt{z}\le 4}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le {x}^{2}-y-z\le 1,\,1\le \sqrt{z}\le 4,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v={x}^{2}-y-z,\,w=\sqrt{z}.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 1,\,1\le w\le 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2x & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2w}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}=-2w.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |-2w|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{4}2w\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}du\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}dv\cdot {\int }_{1}^{4}2w\,dw \\  & =[u]_{u=-2}^{u=2}\cdot [v]_{v=0}^{v=1}\cdot [{w}^{2}]_{w=1}^{w=4} \\  & =(2-(-2))\cdot (1-0)\cdot (16-1) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=4x+16y\,$ on the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
We must find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4,16⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,8y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4=2\lambda x \\ 16=8\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\lambda } \\ y=\frac{2}{\lambda }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=4$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{{\lambda }^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{4}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =4 \\ \frac{4+16}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =4 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =5 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},\,y=\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}),\,(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y)\,$ | $\,(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})\,$ | $\,(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $\,-8\sqrt{5}\,$ | $\,8\sqrt{5}\,$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}),$ and its minimum value is $-8\sqrt{5}.$

questions.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=12x+4\sqrt{6}y\,$ on the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
We must find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=6.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=6
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨12,4\sqrt{6}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨6x,4y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12=6\lambda x \\ 4\sqrt{6}=4\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\lambda } \\ y=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\lambda }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=6$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{4}{{\lambda }^{2}}+2\cdot \frac{6}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =6 \\ \frac{12+12}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =6 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm 1,\,y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-1,-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}),\,(1,\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y)\,$ | $\,(-1,-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2})\,$ | $\,(1,\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2})\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $\,-24\,$ | $\,24\,$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(1,\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}),$ and its maximum value is $24.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/d1a19303937f1d515ca820516e10a73974b00f83884b05abb58dee49c81207f4.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the upper half plane bounded by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ shown above. Given that the mass is distributed uniformly across the plate, find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The area of the plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}=8\pi .
$$

 

Since the mass is distributed uniformly, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{8\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }({\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }({\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}{|}_{0}^{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }\cdot 64\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =4M.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Surface Integrals Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095567/assets/9795c04bf6d4bfa407a7b9176cd5c4b97b3d89bfcc6fff17d1d78190047b3a54.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}6y\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ and whose domain is the upper half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}6y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}6y\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}6y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,6y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,6y\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{Δ}6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\cdot \text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{3}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2\sqrt{3}(1+1) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Using Substitution
questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=6$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(6)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 6\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =3({(3\sqrt{3})}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 27 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the surface ${2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}=2.$ Given that $n=⟨a,b,c⟩$ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(1,-1,1),$ what is the value of $\frac{c}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's define  $f(x,y,z)={2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=2.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy})k \\  & =({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\cdot 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡2)i+({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\cdot 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡2)j+({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\cdot 6z\operatorname{ln}⁡2)k \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2(y\,\text{ }{2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\text{ }i+x\,\text{ }{2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\text{ }j+3z\,\text{ }{2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\text{ }k) \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2((-1)\cdot \text{ }{2}^{3(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}\text{ }i+1\cdot \,\text{ }{2}^{3(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}\text{ }j+3(1)\cdot {2}^{3(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}\text{ }k) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2(-{2}^{1}\text{ }i+{2}^{1}\text{ }j+3\cdot {2}^{1}\text{ }k) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2(-i+j+3\text{ }k) \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,12\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,12\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{c}{b}=\frac{12\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=3.$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨-1,0,x{y}^{3}⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=yz.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,z,y⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & z & y \\ -1 & 0 & x{y}^{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[z(x{y}^{3})-y(0)]i-[0(x{y}^{3})-y(-1)]j+[0(0)-z(-1)]k \\  & =xz{y}^{3}\,i-y\,j+z\,k \\  & =⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =yz⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨4xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4}-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,2) & =⟨4(0)(2)(-1)^{3},-2(-1)^{4}-(-1),2⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡z$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,e].$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡z\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,e].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡z,$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,1\le z\le e,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\operatorname{ln}⁡z,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\frac{1}{z}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\operatorname{ln}⁡z\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\operatorname{ln}⁡z\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0,e)$ to $(1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,e),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e\,\text{d}x+\frac{0}{e}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,e+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0,e)$ to $(1,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-0=1, \\ Δy & =2-e.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (1)+0\cdot (2-e) \\  & ≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $1.$

questions.problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

- ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (-1,1)$
- ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x-t}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (1,2)$
- ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (-1,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(-1,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R$ (since $1+tx>0$). Computing the  partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(1+tx)(1+{x}^{2})}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (-1,1).$

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{1}{x-t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (1,2)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(1,2)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}},
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (1,2).$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that this function is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{3}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{{y}^{3}}{12}+\frac{1}{y}$ that lies between the lines $y=1$ and $y=e.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=1$ to ${y}_{2}=e.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{12}+\frac{1}{y})=\frac{{y}^{4}-4}{4{y}^{2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{\frac{{y}^{8}+8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\,y\sqrt{\frac{({y}^{4}+4)^{2}}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y(\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{4{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}({y}^{3}+\frac{4}{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{{e}^{4}}{4}+4-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}({e}^{4}+15).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $R=[5,6]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le ({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({6}^{2}-{5}^{2})(3-1)=22 \\ \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(6-5)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 22-12\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 10\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=10.
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Express $z=\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=C(t)$ over $[0,15].$ In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is approximated as 

$$
A≈C(3)Δ{t}_{1}+C(7)Δ{t}_{2}+C(12)Δ{t}_{3}+C(15)Δ{t}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $3$ | $7$ | $12$ | $15$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $-$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $3$ |
| $C(t)$ | $-$ | $4$ | $3$ | $5$ | $2$ |

We plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈4\cdot 3+3\cdot 4+5\cdot 5+2\cdot 3 \\  & =12+12+25+6 \\  & =55.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total number of customers served over a period of $15$ minutes. So, the total number of customers is approximately

questions.worked_solution:
The product rule for double summations states that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{j}.
$$

So, using the product rule for double summations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}3{a}_{i}(4-{b}_{j}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}) & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{12}4-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot (4{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}1-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3\cdot 30)\cdot (4\cdot 12-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (48-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (3) \\  & =270\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Simple Sums Over Partitions of the Real Line
questions.problem: Let $P={{z}_{0},{z}_{1},…,{z}_{q}}$ be a partition of the interval $[1,5].$ If $Δ{z}_{k}={z}_{k}-{z}_{k-1},$ calculate ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the factor $3$ outside the summation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}=3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}$ is just the length of the interval $[1,5],$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k} & =({z}_{1}-{z}_{0})+({z}_{2}-{z}_{1})+({z}_{3}-{z}_{2})+⋯+({z}_{q}-{z}_{q-1}) \\  & =(\cancel{{z}_{1}}-{z}_{0})+(\cancel{{z}_{2}}-\cancel{{z}_{1}})+(\cancel{{z}_{3}}-\cancel{{z}_{2}})+⋯+({z}_{q}-\cancel{{z}_{q-1}}) \\  & =-{z}_{0}+{z}_{q} \\  & ={z}_{q}-{z}_{0} \\  & =5-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}=3\cdot 4=12.
$$
